notes.title: Randy Cunningham
notes.body: The hero of Disney XD's Randy Cunningham: 9th Grade Ninja, a freshman who's secretly his town's ninja. People acting undercover are like him.
Pompeii is one of his own songs, a single that's out on streaming. When people said he couldn't sing, he put it out.

notes.title: Ariana Grande
notes.body: The pop singer, named by her last name.
A twist on ride or die. Some people won't ride with you all the way to the end, the hearse.

notes.title: Kobe Bryant
notes.body: Kobe wore 8 for his first ten seasons with the Lakers and 24 for his last ten, and both numbers are retired. Together they make 24/8, a day more than around the clock, which is how much he's there for his family. Frobe is young Kobe, with the afro he had back when he wore 8.

He opens on the house he grew up in: two parents at odds, him at nine already scheming about money, a sibling getting him in trouble. He tells it plainly and with a little humor, which makes it hit harder.
The hook is the center of the song: holding his family tight, and the worry that he's falling short for them. He doesn't settle it. He just names it as part of life.

notes.title: The London
notes.body: Young Thug's 2019 song with J. Cole, named for a hotel in West Hollywood, with Travis Scott singing the hook. London in one line and Travis in the next point at it. 10-4 is radio code for message received.

notes.title: Pepto-Bismol
notes.body: The bright pink stomach medicine. His new sweater is the same shade.

notes.title: GoldLink
notes.body: The Washington, D.C. artist whose 2017 album At What Cost includes the two songs named here, one of them his biggest hit. Then his name turns into the gold chain links he's wearing.

The last verse widens from his own home to a marriage ending in court, where the fight is over money, not the kids. Then he steps back and says this is how families come apart in general, nobody's in particular.
